newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Integration to top east Europe summit agenda.
newsitem.headline: Integration to top east Europe summit agenda.

text.p: Leaders of 16 central and eastern European states will meet in Austria at the weekend to discuss closer regional cooperation and the reconstruction of war-ravaged Bosnia and Croatia, officials said on Thursday.

Issues such as the economic transition of the former East bloc and its future relationship with the European Union would top the agenda, said Austrian diplomats in charge of the two-day summit in the southern town of Graz.
As many as 13 heads of governments from the 15-member Central European Iniative (CEI) group are expected to attend.

The CEI comprises Albania, Austria, Belarus, Bosnia, Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Italy, Macedonia, Poland, Romania, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia and Ukraine. Moldova was expected to be admitted as the 16th member at the weekend.

"The agenda includes the CEI's role in the process of European integration, its contribution to the implementation of the Dayton peace agreement and contributions to the reconstruction of Bosnia and Croatia," Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, the meeting's host, said in a statement.
The CEI was set up in 1989 by four countries to boost European cooperation and regional integration.

The group is supported by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and the EU's PHARE aid programme, from which it draws most of its funds for reconstruction projects in Bosnia and Croatia.
Diplomatic sources said a series of bilateral meetings was likely to round off the agenda of the weekend meeting.

Leaders of the former Yugoslav republics of Croatia and Bosnia are expected to hold talks on the political future of Bosnia, which was split into a shaky Moslem-Croat federation and a Serb-controlled area following last year's Dayton peace accord which ended 43 months of war in the region.

Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn and Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar are likely to continue talks over a disputed Slovak plan to divert Danube river waters for a hydro-electric dam project, officials added.

The Austrian government said both European Commission president Jaques Santer and Hans van den Broek, the EU's special commissioner in charge of eastern Europe, had initially declined invitations to attend the meeting but last-minute efforts were being made to persuade at least one EU commissioner to travel to Austria this weekend.
Most CEI members have signed association agreements with the EU and hope for full membership within the next decade.
Security in Graz, a renaissance town of 200,000 inhabitants surrounded by lush green hills near the Austrian-Slovenian border, was expected to be tight.
"This is a huge affair for Graz," said a spokesman for the Austrian foreign ministry.
